post.caption: The Louvre's golden tiara was brand new. In 1896 the Louvre bought a golden tiara said to be ancient. It was sold as the crown of a Scythian king, and a Greek inscription praised him as great and invincible. The museum paid 200,000 gold francs. The real maker was a goldsmith in Odessa named Israel Rouchomovsky, who was told it was a gift for an archaeologist friend. Experts doubted it because the gold showed no signs of age. The Louvre defended it for six years against the press. In 1903 he rebuilt part of it in front of experts, and the museum took it off display. In 1954 the Louvre showed it again in its Salon of Fakes.
